utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The booths for interpretation are ready. Can everyone hear me? Mr.. Blaskic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can continue then. Mr. Prosecutor, please have the witness brought in who has started to testify. I suppose Mr. Cayley will continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. A point of clarification on the provision of a document to the Defence. Major Baggesen's war diary from Bosnia. My learned friend Mr. Hayman kindly provided me with a letter this morning which he sent to the Registry in November 1996 where he requested a translation of the document from Danish into English. Enquiry has been made with the registry and I understand the position is that the document was provided to them in an original English translation at the end of May 1996. The revised version that was provided yesterday, that is in fact a new document, although that was without any knowledge on our part, so that is just to clarify matters for the purposes of the record. It is the first that we have seen of this document as well. In any event it is our view it does not prejudice the position of the Defence. It is in the form of a record of events as a police officer's notebook would be used. We do not intend to tender it as an exhibit into court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I suggest we see how long the direct examination goes today, your Honour, and that will determine whether any issues are raised. It is true I requested a translation in November 1996, but our records reflect we did not receive anything until yesterday afternoon, whereas it was provided in translated form to the Prosecution in May 1997 and the second or cleaned-up English version apparently perhaps a week ago or more, but let us see how long the direct takes. If there is an issue, we will raise it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The court does not intend to decide whether it will be tendered as evidence or not, but I should like to hear the view of the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Actually, it is a document which should be the object of communication between the parties. The Registrar was required to make a translation; it did do this translation and submitted the translations to the parties that requested it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore the party that asked for the translation, was that the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, in this present case, the person that we made the enquiries with told us that the translation was requested by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore we consider it to be a new exhibit for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The new one is the one that was submitted yesterday that was corrected because there were some errors in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, have you had time to examine this new version of the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We have, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore that means that we have an exhibit translated by the Registry, translation being required by the Defence. This document was given to the Prosecution, and, before any decision is taken as to whether we should admit it into evidence, I propose we continue with the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, and if it is necessary to use this diary in the course of the testimony of the officer, then the Trial Chamber will make a decision as to whether it will be admitted or not. Having regulated that matter, Mr. Cayley, please have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good day, Major. Can you hear me in English, in the language that is easiest for you to follow; can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. You will continue to be examined by the Prosecution, whose witness you are and I wish to remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Cayley, you may proceed. MAJOR LARS BORHOJ BAGGESEN (continued) Examined by MR. CAYLEY (continued)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Major Baggesen, one point: I have been advised by the President to slow down in my asking of questions. If you pause and count 1, 2 in your head before you answer my question, that gives the translation units an opportunity to actually translate what we are saying; so it is my responsibility, I have the problem of regulating the speed but if you could remember that in the course of your testimony. Thank you. Yesterday, we stopped at a point where we were speaking about military communications and specifically the military communications system of the HVO. I would just like you to conclude on that point and answer the question whether or not there was an effective system of military communication between HVO headquarters in Central Bosnia, if you could give your opinion as a professional soldier on that matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion and after my experience as an officer in Denmark for 20 years, what I saw in Bosnia from the HVO side, we saw I think antennas, as I told you yesterday, we saw radio equipment in several places so I think and I can conclude that they were able to communicate effectively with their units from a corps level to brigade level and maybe on to lower levels as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said specifically from a corps level to a brigade level. Could you explain to the court when you use the term "corps" what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By "corps level", I mean from Colonel Blaskic's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was in fact called an operational group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you equating that to a NATO Danish Army term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to a corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could now move on, during the first two weeks in April in Central Bosnia, how would you describe the situation on the ground, the atmosphere in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first period, it seemed calm but there was some tension. There was a lot of shooting. Most of the shooting was due to a lot of drunk soldiers, but later on the tension raised and the incidents were more and more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "drunken soldiers", drunken soldiers of which party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that there were a lot of incidences, what incidences are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Incidences due to snipers killing civilians, burnt houses and looting in the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that during the first few weeks in April, you were briefed by Jean Pierre Thebault, the ECMM ambassador on the Vance-Owen Plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you took a photocopy of a document from a local newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that document with you? Major Baggesen, if you just wait one moment while I hand copies of this document out. Mr. President, if this document could be marked Prosecutor exhibit 88. Major Baggesen has his original copy of the document. It is actually something he would like to keep, so the document which I propose to exhibit with the Registry is a photocopy of that document, although it is a clear and accurate copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the ELMO could be switched on, please? This is a map which I think you photocopied from a local newspaper, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this was a local representation of the proposed Vance-Owen Plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using this map which you produced at the time in Bosnia, can you explain to the court your understanding of the Vance-Owen Plan as it was explained to you by Ambassador Thebault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was a plan to secure the peace and co-operation in Bosnia, and briefly, this plan was made by Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, and it was saying in that plan that Bosnia-Herzegovina had to be shared in ten provinces and each province has to be governed by one of the ethnic groups in Bosnia, so some of the provinces had to be governed by the Bosnian Serbs, some of them have to be governed by the Bosnian Croats and some of them by the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, could you specifically put the pointer towards province 10? This province, what was this province to be called within the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Province number 10, Travnicka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it that was proposed to be the authority in this particular area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have made a note, have you not, at number 10, and I think you have written something next to Travnicka. What have you written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Croats, mixed".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means it was not an ethnic clean province; there were other ethnic groups in that area and most of them were Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying that it was not an exclusive ethnic group at the time in that province; there were other ethnic groups in the province?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify for the record the provinces which were to be part of this Travnik province, the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. Can you hear me now? We have the municipality of Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Fojnica, Gornji Vakuf, Bugojna, Donji Vakuf, Jajce, Kupres, Duvno and Livno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that that province, province 10, actually borders on to the republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that this plan was explained to you, what were your personal views about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal views were not the same as Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen's. I did not like this plan because I did not like to see one ethnic group taking over all the other ethnic groups in the area. I would prefer maybe provinces like this, but governed by a government with all the ethnic groups in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you had real fears about this agreement at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were not only a few who had this opinion, because we were afraid that this -- if those provinces were going to be governed by one of the ethnic groups, it could harm the other ethnic groups in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why could it harm those other ethnic groups in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it would be a lot easier for one ethnic group if you could have an ethnically clean province, because if you have other ethnic groups in that area, that could create problems because they want to have a piece of the cake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So actually, and we were afraid that this could -- that there would be maybe more land-grabbing, so at first -- when one of the ethnic groups had a specific area, they want more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Am I right in saying that the ECMM actively promoted this particular plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now show you another document which you recently provided to me, this will be tendered as Prosecutor's exhibit 89, please, Mr. President. This will be 89A and 89B; it is in French and English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 89A will be the English version and 89B the French version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Cayley, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Major Baggesen, can you identify this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can; that is routine team task, our orders down there telling us what to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were your standard operating procedures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read serial 8 on this document please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serial 8 says that we had to promote the Vance-Owen Peace Plan which encouraged all parties to co-operate by attending provincial and municipal meetings and by offering guidance and interpretation of the plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did. When we had meetings with the local municipalities and the local commanders, we told them about the Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can move on. I would now like you to remember, if you can, the events from 12th April onwards. Just to refresh your memory on what I think is a fairly non-contentious matter, I think you attended, did you not, an Easter celebration at the hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. All the ECMM monitors, we were invited to an Easter celebration party at the HVO headquarters at the hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was present at this party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic, together with Mr. Kordic and most of the HVO commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kordic introduce himself to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say that his position was in the HVO hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He presented himself as the Vice-President of the self-proclaimed republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody make any speeches at this party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I can remember, both Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic gave a speech.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you could not understand the content because they were spoken in the Croatian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes and there was no interpreter close to me so I was not able to hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that M Thebault, the French ambassador, arrived late at the party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He was arriving later because M Thebault was going to Travnik. There had been some tension in Travnik for a few days because the population in Travnik was mixed of Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats had started to flag with the Croatian flag in Travnik, and the Muslims in that area did not want the Croatian flag in Travnik. Therefore the Ambassador went to Travnik to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify this point for the transcript, you say that the Bosnian Croats had raised the Croatian flag in Travnik and this had upset the Muslims in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ambassador Thebault actually get into Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not, because on the way to Travnik, he was stopped at the Puticevo checkpoint where the HVO soldiers at the checkpoint aimed their weapons against him and they did not allow him to pass the checkpoint and go to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, there is a map next to you on the easel. Could you take a look at it and see if you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I would like you to do is to take one of the pens that is next to you on the TV screen and mark on that map -- use one of the markers, please. If you would mark on the map the location of the Puticevo checkpoint near Travnik. If you could mark it with a cross --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Too late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With a circle, that is fine. If you could mark it "HVO" to indicate that it was an HVO checkpoint. If you could stay up there, while we are on checkpoints, from recollection could you mark in a red pen the location on that exhibit of every permanent HVO checkpoint that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we have a time reference, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For the period of time that you were serving in the former Yugoslavia, which I think is the only period you can give any evidence for, so from April to June 1993 the permanent checkpoints that you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ones I was going to mark on here was permanent checkpoints in that area that were there for the whole period of my time there. Those checkpoints I am going to mark on the map are those checkpoints who were manned during my period and it was all checkpoints that were there every day during my period. There were a lot of other checkpoints, but they were only manned during special occasions. The Puticevo checkpoint manned by HVO --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I approach the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I do not know if my learned colleague wishes to come in any closer? Major Baggesen, can you identify the geographical location on the map of the checkpoint, of each one, so the one at the top?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one at the top is the Puticevo checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one that you just marked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are on the entrance to one of the roads to Vitez, and the next one is the Dubravica checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the Dubravica checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then there was another checkpoint in this area, but I cannot remember exactly the position, but somewhere here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put a larger circle and for the purposes of the transcript, this is an approximation of the location of the checkpoint. Major Baggesen, will you take this blue pen and, for the purposes of accuracy and truth, can you place on there the locations of the Bosnian army checkpoints that you were aware of in the three-month period of April to June 1993 in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that. There was one, I cannot remember -- BiH checkpoint here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are marking that "BiH" to identify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Those were BiH checkpoints. I cannot remember if this was there the whole time, but I know we passed a checkpoint there several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major Baggesen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then there were checkpoints at the Busovaca road; I cannot remember the exact places. There were checkpoints in the Kiseljak area, down in this area, but I cannot remember exactly the places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will not put them in if you cannot remember the more or less exact locations. Thank you. Major Baggesen, what was the importance of those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The importance of checkpoints was for the ones who had the checkpoint to control all traffic in that area, ingoing and outgoing traffic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your experience on the ground, were they actually effective at doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, going back to the Easter celebrations, that you yourself attempted to actually go to Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together with a German monitor, Mr. Dieter Schellschmidt, we wanted to go up there. At first the ambassador did not want us to go up there. He thought it was too dangerous for us to go up there because of the tensions in that area, but because we were military persons we thought it was necessary to monitor the situation, so we went to that checkpoint to monitor what was happening up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the pointer, can you indicate to the court broadly where you were travelling from and to and the location of Zenica, just so we can all orientate ourselves to the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenica is situated here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was the headquarters of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This particular day we were in the Vitez at the HVO headquarters at hotel Vitez. We travelled this road to the checkpoint up here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a seat. So you travelled this road from Vitez. Can you tell the court what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On our way to the checkpoint, there was nothing outside Vitez, there was no problem, but approximately 1 kilometre before we reached the checkpoint, we saw a military unit, maybe a headquarters, on the right side of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you. Which checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The checkpoint near Travnik we were going to have a look at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this military unit, maybe a headquarters, we saw the Croatian flag raised in front of the building and a black flag with a skull and two crossbones were there as well. This last-mentioned flag, the pirate flag, was normally used by soldiers from the HOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ECMM view on these HOS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our view or our military view on the HOS units was that they were better equipped and they were better trained. Normally they were the units who were doing special operations, if I can use that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you form an opinion about whose command these troops fell under?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no doubt to us that they were under command of Colonel Blaskic, because normally -- that is normal in the military way, when you are having a command over a certain area of responsibility, then you will have automatically a command over all the military units in that area, and therefore this HOS units operated in the area which were under the command of Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you get past these soldiers in this checkpoint near Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived to a checkpoint, I can remember that it was manned by HVO soldiers and we could see it was HVO soldiers because of the badge on the soldiers. There were soldiers there in black uniforms. The soldiers in black uniforms we discussed, because normally the HOS soldiers were in black uniforms but I cannot remember if we saw the HOS sign on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you pass the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I cannot remember if we passed the checkpoint, but I can remember that when we went back, we took another way back to Zenica and it seemed calm. There were a lot of smaller checkpoints, but there was no problem passing those checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now go forward in time to 14th April, and again you can use your diary to refresh your memory, I think a complaint was made at the Busovaca Joint Commission by the HVO at that time about the kidnapping of four staff officers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We learnt that four staff officers --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could pause a moment, Major Baggesen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I just have some clarification? You said the HOS were for special missions. What were these special missions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those special missions, and I use the expression "special operations", we were told that those were the units who did some of the crime against the law of armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Some of the crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What do you call "crimes against --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Killing of civilians, looting houses, burning houses, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I can just refresh your memory, 14th April, the kidnapping of four staff officers in Travnik and Novi Travnik. Complaint was made by Colonel Blaskic's representatives at the joint commission, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain the complaint that was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that four HVO staff officers were kidnapped close to a front in the Travnik area and we were told that by HVO, that they thought it was 7, a Muslim brigade, who was behind this kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do as a result of this complaint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We made a special investigation team with the Spanish deputy we had at the RC Zenica, Juan Valentin and me and, together with Franjo Nakic from HVO and Mr. Merdan from BiH, we went out to investigate this kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to visit 7 Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we went to the headquarters of the 7th Muslim Brigade, who were situated in the mountains near Bugojna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just, again for the purpose of orientation, indicate on the map (i) where the staff officers were kidnapped and (ii) the journey you took to Bugojna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitez is situated here, Travnik in this area, and we were told that the HVO officers were kidnapped in this area. Therefore we took our way to Bugojna who is situated down in this area, and the headquarters of the 7th Muslim Brigade are somewhere out here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Baggesen. When you got to the headquarters of the 7th Muslim Brigade, what did they tell you about these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a meeting with representatives from the brigade and they told us they were not behind this kidnapping, and we discussed the matter, but they refused to have anything to do with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they behave towards you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually we have heard a lot of rumours about this 7th Muslim Brigade. We heard they were very Islamic, but we were surprised; they were very polite to us. I do not think we actually trusted them 100 per cent, but they were acting very polite and very disciplined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After you received this answer from the 7th Muslim Brigade, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went back and on our way back we visited the local HVO brigade commander in Novi Travnik, Mr. Sabljic to tell him about our findings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there were some other people there as well, were there not, from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we have told Mr. Sabljic about our findings, the commander of the military HVO police came into the brigade commander's office and we told him about our findings as well, and then this military police commander went very angry because we have not found out anything. Then he said that the only way to solve the problem was to arrest Mr. Merdan, who was a senior representative from BiH and a member of the investigation team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the commander of the HVO military police suggested that the only solution was to arrest Dzemal Merdan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Nakic who was a member of the investigation team who we were told was Mr. Blaskic's deputy, and Mr. Sabljic, the local brigade commander, they were not able to do anything because we complained to them that they have to do something and tell something to this military police commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the military police commander arrest Mr. Merdan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and then we told him that Mr. Merdan was under our protection and he will leave the office and Novi Travnik together with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, if you could slow down a little bit for the purposes of interpretation. What did the HVO military police commander say when you said that Mr. Merdan was going to leave the office with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he told us that then he would have to arrest us as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he serious about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He seems very serious and he put a guard with us and this guard, he cocked his rifle so he was guarding us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "cocking his rifle", you mean that the guard put a round of ammunition in the chamber of the weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you take the threat seriously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do at this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were allowed to make a phone call from the office and while I, Mr. Nakic or Mr. Sabljic were able to command this military police officer, we tried to get in contact with Mr. Blaskic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you there? You said: "While I, Mr. Nakic or Mr. Sabljic were able to command this military police ..." Did you mean you were not able?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were not able, because we were told the only one who had command over the military police was Mr. Blaskic himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through our interpreter we tried to get in contact with Colonel Blaskic. We did not succeed on our first call, but we heard that he was present but actually he was having a shower. After that, we tried to get in contact with our own headquarters in Zenica and we told the duty officer at our own headquarters about the situation and we asked him to get in contact with the British UNPROFOR battalion and ask for their help so they could come and get us out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was the Cheshire regiment located in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Part of the United Nations Protection Force in Bosnia. How did the head of the military police react when you said that the UN Protection Force were coming to assist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told us that if the UNPROFOR unit would come to get us out, his unit will open fire against the UNPROFOR units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you call Colonel Blaskic back on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and actually we succeeded to have a contact with Colonel Blaskic and our interpreter told him about the situation, and then Colonel Blaskic asked to have a conversation with the military police commander, and after a while, the military police commander did not want to continue the conversation in the office where we were able to listen, so he went to another office to continue the conversation with Colonel Blaskic, and after a while, he came back and released us. He was very red in his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very red in the face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a military man, what did it look like to you had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We normally call it a military conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. After this, were you released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were released and we could go back to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With Mr. Merdan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Mr. Merdan and the rest of the team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that after this event, part of the road in the area was closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, after that it was ordered by the Commander of HVO, Colonel Blaskic, that the route from Travnik to Gornji Vakuf had to be closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that as a result of the kidnapping of the four staff officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that was the result and I can remember that there was made another roadblock by civilians, all relatives to the four kidnapped officers because they were, as well as we, all were disappointed that we have not found out anything yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although this moves ahead quite some period in time, can you explain to the court ultimately what happened in respect of those four HVO staff officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on, I cannot recall the exact date --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April, later in April, at our headquarters in Zenica, the ECMM headquarters in Zenica, we had a representative from Mujahedins, Muslim extremists, who came to us and gave us a letter. In this letter, the Mujahedins told us that they had the four, or later on five, kidnapped officers. Before this took place, another HVO brigade commander were kidnapped in Zenica. He was commanding one of the HVO brigades in Zenica and he was stopped. The four bodyguards who were travelling with him in his car were killed by a shot in the head. An eyewitness only 100 metres from that spot was killed as well, so at this time, the Mujahedins had now five kidnapped officers. When we had this letter, the Mujahedins told us that now we were responsible for releasing I think it was 15 of their Muslim brothers who were kept by HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why had all these staff officers been kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually because HVO had arrested a lot of Mujahedins and now the Mujahedins want to have something to deal with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an exchange arranged by ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we started to negotiate with the Mujahedins and with HVO, and at last all the kidnapped officers were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all safe and healthy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After conditions, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Mujahedin, were they in good condition when they were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that concludes that event. If we could now return to 15th April, these staff officers are still in custody, they have not yet been released, so you are continuing your investigations to find out where they are. I think on 15th April you travelled to Vitez from Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this time you had a British battalion escort you because the circumstances were dangerous. There was a lot of shooting and you were unarmed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, normally as I told the court yesterday, we were unarmed and we were poorly protected and at that time, we were shot at very often by both parts, I do not think it was to kill us, just to scare us, and we needed armoured protection to do our job, so therefore the rest of the time when I was down there, we had to go in armoured vehicles from the British battalion, the Canadian battalion or the Danish battalion in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that that evening you decided to stay in Vitez, on the evening of 15th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, because we felt not secure going from Vitez to Zenica, because the tension in the area at that time was very high, there was a lot of shooting in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stayed at the ECMM house next to the British battalion headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there was also a problem with your vehicle, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, actually our vehicle broke down, the clutch was destroyed, so we were not able to -- we were only able to drive 20 miles a hour or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court in your own words of the events of the morning of 16th April, at what time you woke and what you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We woke up early in the morning because there was heavy shelling in that area. We could hear a lot of shooting with machine-guns, heavy machine-guns; we could hear outgoing rounds from artillery and outgoing rounds from mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a professional soldier. These weapons have a very distinctive sound; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you heard heavy machine-gun fire. You also said you heard mortar fire. Is it possible from the sound of a mortar to actually estimate the calibre or size of that mortar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because of this special noise; you can hear if it is a light mortar, a medium mortar or a heavy mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the sound is created by the shell being dropped into the mortar barrel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It hits the base of the mortar barrel and then ignites, there is an explosion and the shell comes from the barrel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to estimate the size of mortar that was being used, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We agreed that it was not a light mortar; it was more a medium or maybe a heavy mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the artillery fire, again the shell from a piece of artillery, does it make a distinctive sound, depending on the size?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bigger noise --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bigger the bang, the bigger the weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this time we thought it was a medium artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was this in the morning, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very early, I think about 5.30 or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you received information from the British battalion about military positions in the area and weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally because we were living so close to the British battalion, we were just living outside the entrance to their barracks, normally we went to their informations office and asked them what kind of military units were in those areas where we were going to, and we learnt during one of these meetings with the British battalion that HVO had some positions where they had mortars and artillery in that area surrounding the BritBat camp and the ECMM house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, can you slow down in your speech? I will do my best as well. Go much, much slower so the interpreters can give an accurate translation. You said that the British battalion informed you that the HVO had positions where they had mortars and artillery in this area. What did they tell you about the Bosnian army in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not and UNPROFOR at that time did not know anything about BiH positions in that area. We have not seen anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "did not know anything about", do you mean that they did not know anything or that there were no positions in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were no -- because we have been in the area, UNPROFOR have been in the area, and we have seen no signs of BiH positions in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about weaponry of any BiH that might have been in the area? What did they tell you about the weaponry of those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only small arms and light machine-guns, so no big arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "big arms", what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Heavy machine-gun and artillery and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the Prosecutor could now tender exhibit 56A? This is an exhibit that has already been admitted into evidence. It is an aerial photograph, but this is a paper copy of that photograph, because the witness may make some marks. We do not want to mark the original version, and we can arrange for a copy of that paper copy to be given to the Defence. Mr. Usher, if you could? (Handed). Major Baggesen, remembering that speed is everything, could you take a look at that aerial photograph and see if you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a photograph of Vitez and the roads in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that the ECMM house is not actually marked on that photograph, in fact it is not depicted on the photograph, but if you could stand up and indicate sort of approximately where it would have been located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do. We have Vitez situated here (indicating) and the normal road we used -- Vitez is situated here and we have the road from Zenica and to Travnik, this one. The ECMM house and the British battalion were down in this area here, outside this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I approach the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. If the Defence wants to they can do so as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you tried to leave Vitez that morning and return to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Because of all the shooting and all the fire with mortars, artillery and heavy machine-guns, we did not feel safe in Vitez, therefore we wanted to travel back to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was in a vehicle with a non-serviceable clutch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were travelling pretty slowly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it was an armoured vehicle so we were -- we felt safe in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate on the map the route that you took past Vitez on the way back to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the way back to Zenica, we took this road as normal, up in this direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are pointing to the road to the left of the central road running through Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is, as it were, a bypass road. Did you actually -- wait one moment. Did you actually see anything on that road as you were travelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we were travelling in this direction, we were able to see smoke from this area, the distance from here to here is approximately 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the distance between the road that you were travelling on and the area from which you could see smoke was approximately 1 kilometre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate with this red pen approximately, and I say that for the purposes of the transcript, the area where you could see smoke rising?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot pinpoint one house, but I can say it was in this area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark that with this red pen. Can you mark that 1, can you put a 1 by it? It might be an idea if you put the date in as well, which is 16th April, and the approximate time of day, as best you can remember. Did you discuss with your colleague the smoke that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember if we discussed it because it happened so often that we were passing a village where there was smoke because the house was burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the smoke actually indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That there were some houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you travelled on up that road, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we travelled up this road and I cannot remember exactly the place, but we found a place where there were some persons lying down at the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of persons lying on the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Persons in civilian clothes, maybe civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we tried to get out of our vehicle to investigate that, we were shot at by soldiers in HVO uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you got back into the vehicle and continued on up the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we continued up the road in this direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not because we were stopped in the Dubravica checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate where the Dubravica checkpoint is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Dubravica checkpoint is situated in this junction here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take this blue marker and just mark on there where that is? You are marking it "HVO Checkpoint", and it is a blue circle. Did you get through the Dubravica checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not because the soldiers there told us that it was too dangerous for us to travel further in that direction because of the heavy fightings in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there -- how many soldiers were there at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day there were more soldiers at the checkpoint than normal. The normal picture was that there were two, maybe three, soldiers at the checkpoint, but this morning there were maybe ten soldiers at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It indicated that something was going on, maybe a military operation in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Baggesen. Thank you, Mr. President. They refused to allow you to pass; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no other way to go to Zenica, so we went back to Vitez and we continued an investigation in the case with the four kidnapped officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any calls from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we came back to our house in Vitez, we received a call from the duty officer at our headquarters in Zenica, and he told us that our headquarters had been contacted by the commander of the Serbs, Bosnian Corps, asking us to contact Colonel Blaskic and ask for a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try and contact Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We tried several times but we were told that Colonel Blaskic was not in at his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were with a fellow army officer at the time, I think a lieutenant-colonel, am I right, from the Canadian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss this lack of presence of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did and we found out that maybe we were not that surprised that we were not able to get in contact with Colonel Blaskic, because it is normal during a military operation that the commander is at the forward headquarters so he can be closer to the front and command his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is normal for a commander to be at his forward headquarters to command his operation on the ground and you were calling the hotel Vitez which was a rear or central headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that that day, the British battalion based in Vitez, outside Vitez, had patrols out on the ground in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally BritBat had patrols out in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think they were receiving or giving you information about what was going on out on the ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try and get back to Zenica again that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later on when it was dark, we tried to go back to Zenica, using the same road as we tried to use this morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please stand up again, Major Baggesen, and just for the sake of clarity indicate on the map the road that you were taking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I do it from here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had our headquarters in Vitez down here and we took this way (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was that, this second attempt to leave Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact time. Yes, I have it here, 9.30, and I can remember it was dark at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court what you could see as you were travelling down this road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were able to see that there was still some fire in this part of Vitez. We were able to see that in the dark because all the fires in that area illuminated the sky. We were able to see that there was a lot of firing with machine-guns because -- that is easy to see when it is dark because of all the traces in the air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court so that we are all clear what tracer fire is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tracer fire is, normally, when you are firing a machine gun or a heavy machine-gun, every five or ten rounds have a piece of phosphorous in the back of the projectile so you are able when you are shooting in the dark to see the curve of the projectiles. It is easier for the men who are using the weapon to see the targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in effect you can see lightning rods across the sky as every fifth or tenth round has this phosphorus in the round?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you could clearly see the direction of fire, can you explain to the court what you could actually see, where the firing was coming from and where it was going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were able to see that the firing came from different positions but all in the same direction, and we were only able to see fire going in one direction, we were not able to see that someone was firing back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That this was -- there was only one part who was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not know if you wish to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is time for a break. We will resume work at 11.40. (11.20 am) (A short break) (11.40 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. One point, Mr. President, has arisen in the break. I have been informed by the translation unit that there was a small error in a translation from the English into the Bosnian Serbo-Croat, and that was in respect of the description that Major Baggesen gave to a conversation that took place in Travnik on the telephone between Colonel Blaskic and the HVO military police commander. He stated that he believed, or his opinion was, that a military conversation had taken place and I understand that the translation that Mr. Nobilo and Colonel Blaskic received is that there was not a military conversation, so it is in the positive rather than the negative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. If both parties agree, I am going to ask the Registrar to confirm in the transcript this correction of the error. I must also say I did not wish to interrupt, but you are having a military conversation and there seems to be a kind of complicity between you, as if this was a conversation among military people. I did not wish to interrupt because I know that it may mean many things. I do not suppose it is so very important, but it seems to be conducted between you. I am not mistaken, am I, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I suppose that military people do speak in a certain manner, your Honour. I am a humble military Prosecutor, but I do have some military knowledge. What I will try and do, and I hope I have done that already, is to explain when military terminology is used. It is important, it is relevant; this is a trial of an army officer after all, and I am doing my best to try and explain military terms to lay people. I am not an expert myself; Major Baggesen is more of an expert or is an expert in matters of weaponry and communications, but I will remember, Mr. President, from now on what you have said and try and simplify language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. We are only humble judges and not military experts. We can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, for the purposes of the record, you marked on the map 0600 hours. What was that time that you have indicated on the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was, as I can remember, the time when we were driving at the road, passing Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to recall, 15th and 16th April when you were present in this area, did you see any Bosnian government forces at the time, any Bosnian army units on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Remembering again that speed is everything, and also explaining military terminology to the court, we will continue. I will stop you if I am nudged by my colleagues here that a term has been used that may not be clear to the court. I think the time is now approximately 2130 hours. It is 10.30 in the evening, and you are travelling on this road, this bypass road through Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get past the checkpoint at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we passed the checkpoint and there was no problem at that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other checkpoints in the region of that checkpoint you have marked on that aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was another checkpoint in the neighbourhood that controlled the road from one road down to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you again mark that on that aerial photograph with the same marker that you did before? You might wish to mark that "HVO 2". If you could put "HVO CP2", just to distinguish it from the other mark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This checkpoint normally controlled the traffic on the road from the main road and into Vitez, so we do not have to pass this checkpoint when we were using the before-mentioned road, only if we have to go from the junction to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the direction of Zenica, taking into account these two checkpoints you have marked, who controlled access in and out of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You successfully negotiated the checkpoint on this occasion. Where did you go to after this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We tried to go back to Zenica because we felt more secure in Zenica. When we were coming closer to Zenica and outside this photo, we were able to see that the whole sky was illuminated by a big fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could wait, Major Baggesen, at this point? Mr. President, I would like to tender exhibit 50A which again is a photographic copy of an exhibit that we have previously tendered before the court, the purpose again being because the witness is going to mark this photographic copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could you give me the number, the exact number of the original exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore the original exhibit is 50, and for the needs of this testimony, we are going to work on a photocopy which will also be admitted under which number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: To facilitate our work, we are going to call it 50A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Everybody is agreed? Very well. Continue, please, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Major Baggesen, can you take a look at this aerial photograph next to you? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, again if I can ask the indulgence of the court, if I could approach the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Also the Defence may do that if they wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you indicate to the court the road on which you travelled on the way back to Zenica? What villages does that road pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court what you saw as you drove down that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were driving along this road from Vitez to the Zenica area and when we came down here, we were able to see that this area here was illuminated and we could see there was a big fire going on. Actually, when we came closer, we could see that the whole area was on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find the source of the fire, where the fire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because when we came up here, we could see that the area here was on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take the red marker and indicate the area? Is this approximately, this is not exact, the area that you can identify here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very difficult; we could just see that the whole area was burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark with that red pen the area that you saw was burning? You have marked a red circle on the aerial photograph. That is the area that you believe was burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, maybe more, because there was a lot of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman cannot see, so could you make it a bit clearer? You were about to say something. Maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it was a bigger area. It was very difficult to see because of all the fires in there, but I can remember it was an awful sight because at that time we had seen a lot of single houses on fire but this time it was a whole area that was burning. At that time, there was a beautiful mosque and we were able to see at that time that the minaret was still up and we were able to see this minaret illuminated from all the fires around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The minaret of the mosque was still standing and it was illuminated by this fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe the size of this fire to make it clear to the court, the extent, the area it was covering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my point of view, it was to see a whole village on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try and enter the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We tried to go in here (indicating) to monitor the situation, but we were stopped at a checkpoint here (indicating), as I can remember. There was only one, maybe two, soldiers who denied us access to that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the checkpoint manned by? What soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO, and we could see that because they were wearing HVO badges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark on the map the location of that checkpoint in blue; that is fine. You might want to mark it "HVO". So you have marked, for the purposes of the transcript, a blue circle indicating that there was an HVO checkpoint on the main road next to the side road going into the village of Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the soldiers at this checkpoint give you a reason why you could not go into the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were told that it was an unsafe area for us to go into because there were heavy fightings in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They said there was heavy fighting in the area. Did you see any sign of fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we saw from the road -- we were able to look up at the road and we saw some persons at the ground, close to the road, maybe bodies, maybe persons who were just lying down; we were not able to see if it was bodies. One of the houses were illuminated. They all were, but in one of them we were able to see a person laying in the window, maybe a body, maybe a person who was on his way in or out of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were looking up the road and it was difficult to see; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The damage that you saw in the village, this fire, again you are a professional army officer, and, remembering to keep the language simple, did you discuss with your fellow officer how that fire had been started in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because a fire like this could not have been started because there have been used artillery or mortars, so we discussed and concluded that this was a fire that was put on by humans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying that somebody had physically started the fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was not a result of use of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that you had visited Ahmici before this time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact day; it was a few days before this happened. Normally we passed Ahmici when we were going from Zenica to Vitez, and one of my interpreters told me one day that we have to visit Ahmici, so I could see the mosque, because the people in Ahmici were very proud of their new mosque. It was mostly a new-built mosque. The people in Ahmici had raised the money themselves for this mosque. My interpreter asked me to go up there to have a look, because normally I am interested in architecture. We went up and I saw the mosque and it was a beautiful mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the village appear to you on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very calm. The children were playing in the street, we were able to hear the birds singing and it was very calm in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any signs of military fortifications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any wire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any artillery positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw nothing. It seems that Ahmici was -- you are not able to see that there was a war going on when you visit Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: A bit more slowly, please, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. So you saw no sign of any military activity when you visited Ahmici a few days before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no sign of military activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to conclude on these days, the attack that you had seen on Vitez and the aftermath, the results of the attack on Ahmici, what were the conclusions that you reached about this matter as a professional soldier in discussion with your colleagues in ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We concluded that this was a military operation, but not against a military target, but against a civilian target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that a report was actually made in writing about this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We made a lot of reports, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would like to tender an exhibit. Mr. Dubuisson, what number will this be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could tender exhibit 90? (Handed). I apologise, Mr. President, there is not a translation into the French language, but I will get the witness to read out the relevant paragraph. Much of this is actually irrelevant, but in the interests of totality I admit the whole document. Do you recognise this document, Major Baggesen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this document is an ECMM weekly summary and this is a document which was weekly made at our headquarters in Zagreb. It was a summary of all the reports from the Regional Centres in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to paragraphs 14 and 15? If you could pause one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand that this document actually provides summaries of events, in fact all across Bosnia and in Croatia I think, and also in Hungary and Albania where there were officers of the ECMM; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a summary of the region reports from the ECMM in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read paragraph 15 of the summary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it says: "The declared position of the Bosnian Croat authorities to implement the Vance-Owen Plan, forcing the Muslim population to leave the so-called Croat provinces, provoked a reaction which resulted in strong and brutal fighting with action against the civilian population, especially in the Zenica and Vitez regions."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that conclusion reached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because what we were able to see there was military actions, military activities against the civilian Muslim population in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that what you saw on 15th and 16th April was the result of some uprising by two or three soldiers who just decided to take matters into their own hands, attack the Vitez and Ahmici area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is no doubt that this was a military operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the area into Vitez sealed at the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was sealed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the traffic was being controlled going in and out of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say it was a military operation. What was the purpose of this military operation in your view? I know you have read the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We think that this operation, military operation, against the civilian population was to scare them and to show what would happen if other villages and the Muslim inhabitants in other villages if they do not move out. So I think this was an example to show.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give an estimate of the number of men that you believe would have been required to carry out this size of operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would think maybe 500 to 600 soldiers to do this operation in Vitez and Ahmici area. This would include the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it have to have co-ordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when you have a big operation like this, it had to be co-ordinated because you have to use different units and you have to command those units, because there is a lot of -- you have to transport the soldiers to the area, you have to do all the logistic stuff when you are carrying out operations like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "logistics", you mean military supplies, ammunition, fuel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, one moment, Mr. President. (Pause). I think you left Ahmici that evening not having been able to get into the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you returned to the city of Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move forward in time, and again you may refresh your memory from your diary, to 19th April. What happened in Zenica on 19th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
