utterances.text: The day started as usual but in the morning the city was attacked without any warning by artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at the time this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At our headquarters in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually respond to this shelling of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. After the shelling, I went down to the area that had been hit, together with another Danish monitor, Allan Laustsen, who is a former artillery officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So an officer familiar with heavy weapons, with heavy guns, and the ammunition used by those guns; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, normally all officers in the Danish Army are familiar with the use of artillery. It is a part of our officers' training.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could tender exhibit 91? Mr. Usher? (Handed). Could you explain to the court what this photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph is a photograph I took the same day at the marketplace in Zenica. It shows one of the impacts in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a point where one of these shells fell in the city.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately what time these shells fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is what the ground looked like where one of these shells fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could you tell by looking at this crater with your expert eye?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally when we are seeing an impact like this, we are able to see what direction it came from and we can -- it all depends on how the ground are. We are able to see what kind of artillery that were used there, how big a cannon was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to do that with this crater?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, specifically on this crater because it is very easy on this one to see the direction from the firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court, using a pointer, how you came to that conclusion, remembering again that many people in here are not from a military background. Can you explain how you worked out the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can see that the grenade or the shell hits just here, and then there is a lot of splashmarks out in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The splashmarks, you call them "splashmarks"; I know that again is a term that is used. What are they caused by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are caused by the shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They are caused by the shrapnel that flies out from the shell. Is that a normal pattern made by a shell when it hits the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when it hits on the road like here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate with the pointer from what direction the shell was coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was coming from this direction, and it hits here, it explodes and all the splash goes in this direction, to those two sides here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are no splashmarks behind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, so therefore this -- it is very easy, we were logging it and it was very easy for us to see the direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to use the information that you saw on the ground to work out on the map from which direction the shell had been fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because we were using our compass, and using that we were able to put it on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a compass with you at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just demonstrate to the court the exercise that you went through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I showed with the pointer, it was easy to see the direction. Then we took our compass and put it in there and then we were able to see the direction and from this it was easy to see that the direction was 270 degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is broadly, on the four compass points, from a westerly direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not going to ask you to stand up and look at the map again, but from your recollection what was in a westerly direction from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An area under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The range of the shell, the distance that it can be fired, obviously has an effect as well on the possible location of where the firing is coming from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and this type of artillery was being used here. We discussed and we concluded that it had to be medium artillery, that is a 122 millimetre artillery. Normally you use them on a distance of 14 or 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could you tell what size of artillery it was, that it was a 122 millimetre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just like you can hear on the noise, the bigger the bang, the bigger --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Basically a bigger hole in the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same here, from the size of the hole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to correct matters, can you state again the size that you estimated the artillery shell was that hit the ground in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 122 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you estimated that the range was 14 to 15 kilometres and that it had been fired from a westerly direction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could obviously look at a map and pinpoint an area 15 kilometres from Zenica in a westerly direction. Where did that take you on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To an area controlled by HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of that area, broadly speaking between two towns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you stand up and look at the map and if the usher could assist you by flipping over the aerial photograph that is covering the map, you may be able to refresh your memory from the map. Mr. President, may I approach the witness? Can you indicate where Zenica is on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenica is here and a western direction from Zenica is to this area over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a westerly direction. This is an approximation, is it not; it is not an exact science.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you estimate that the shells came from? Where did you and Allan Laustsen estimate that the shells had been fired from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the area over here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you specify what that area is on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the Bila area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Bila area on the map. That is in the top mid-point on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally we call this area the Bila area and that was at that time controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We concluded it was HVO, we were not able to have a look at -- there was no name on the shells, but we did not think that BiH were going to shell their own town. Later on Zenica was shelled by the Bosnian Serb Army, but that was from another direction from an area north of Travnik and there was no doubt that this was from this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These shots that were fired into Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, can you repeat this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have just said, have you not, Major Baggesen that you concluded it was the HVO, but you did not think that the Bosnian army were going to shell their own town; is that correct? Then you said that later on the Bosnian Serb Army shelled Zenica, but that was from another direction that was north of Travnik and that there was no doubt in your mind that these shells --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Were from the HVO area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This shelling, was it aimed at a military target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not able to see any military targets in that area where the shells were, where all the impacts were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were military targets in Zenica, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but not at the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these shells fell in the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nodded).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe they were aimed shots, that they were actually targetting a specific area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After what we have seen down there, the men, the soldiers, who were manning the artillery pieces were badly trained and I do not think they were able to hit a target with that precision as we normally see good trained soldiers could do, so we think this was just a terror-bombing against the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Terror-bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a military word again, I am sorry, but an artillery attack against a civilian target would be proposed to scare people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think they wanted to scare people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, there was a minority of Bosnian Croats who were living in Zenica and this could be the reason for HVO to do this attack, maybe to scare the Croat inhabitants in Zenica out of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why would they want to frighten the Croat inhabitants of Zenica into leaving the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they want them to go to the 10th province; I am referring to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. We saw later on examples that HVO were doing a lot of things to get Croats out of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were moving the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Mr. President. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I am sorry to try to ask for a clarification. You said they were trying to move out the Croat population. I did not understand why they should move them out? Was it as a preparation for an attack of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I think that this was done because they want as many Croats in the 10th province as possible, therefore they want to move all the Croats out of Zenica so the majority in the 10th province could be Croats. You can see this together with they were doing all those ethnic cleansing from the 10th province, so they were scaring the Muslim population out of the 10th province and they were taking Croat people from the Zenica area who were belonging to the 9th province to the 10th province.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: By scaring both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse us, Mr. Cayley. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify that point that Judge Riad has asked, Zenica itself was in the 9th province of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and the border between the 9th and the 10th province was the border between the Vitez, Travnik and Busovaca -- the borders between those municipalities and Zenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Zenica municipality, or the Zenica province within the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, who was to control that under the Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I can now tender Prosecutor's exhibit 91?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies, 92. If I could tender Prosecutor's exhibit 92? The photograph is 91. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, which is 92? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, can you turn to the second page of this document? Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not want you to read this report, but it concerns the events of 25th April 1993. If you could summarise to the court what happened, indicating on the map the locations of where these events happened? This, I think, involved a visit by you with another monitor to villages just south of Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were accompanied by Father Stjepan, who was a Roman Catholic priest from Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court how this visit to these villages south of Zenica came about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The day before this happened, around 24th April, there was a lot of rumours in Zenica, rumours from the Croats telling that Muslims were going to attack and kill all the Croats in Zenica and in the small villages around Zenica. Therefore a lot of the Croat population in Zenica and the small villages around Zenica escaped. They all escaped to a village called Grahovcici and our main task was to get many of those refugees back to their own houses. Therefore a Dutch monitor, Henk Morsink, and I together with Father Stjepan went out to visit those villages where the refugees came from to see if there were any problems in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate on the map just broadly -- the judges will not be able to see it -- where Zenica is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenica is situated here (indicating) and all the villagers were from small villages out in this area here (indicating) and he went to a place called Grahovcici in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These small villages south of Zenica, who was that area controlled by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This area, controlled by BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the Bosnian army. Were they villages with a mixed ethnic population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of the villages were mixed population with Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that as a result of rumours, these people fled to Grahovcici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that controlled by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit these small villages just south of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did and we found that there was no problems except for in one of the villages where some of the houses had been robbed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in one of the villages, some of the houses belonging to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the Bosnian Croats had been robbed, but what about in the other villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no problem and we interviewed the Muslim neighbours to the Croats in the area and we told them that there was no problem and they wanted their neighbours back because they had friendly relations with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were told in two of the villages, Stranjani and Janjac, that several houses had been burnt down and an old lady had been killed by sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember if we saw the burnt houses, but it was normal down there to see burnt houses. In every village there were burnt houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your feeling generally about these villages is that things were fairly peaceful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not only our opinion, it was Father Stjepan's opinion as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Roman Catholic priest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the Bosnian Muslims living in these villages say about their Bosnian Croat neighbours? Did they want them back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they wanted them back because they had good relations with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together with Father Stjepan we went to Grahovcici where we had a meeting with representatives from the small villages and we told them, or Father Stjepan told them, about our findings and we told them that it was safe for them to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many refugees were there in Grahovcici?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2,000 refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did they say they had fled from their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they have heard the rumour that the Muslims were going to kill them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say who told them these rumours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It came from other Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make arrangements to return these Bosnian Croats to their homes in these villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, actually this arrangement was thought of by us but fulfilled by Father Stjepan who found some civilian buses from Zenica to go to Grahovcici the next day to bring them home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did everything go to plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the beginning, because the next day we went to Grahovcici but at an HVO checkpoint, temporary checkpoint, in Novi Selo, we were stopped, and the commander there, he took the buses from us and we were not allowed to go to Grahovcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the HVO checkpoint in Grahovcici, the HVO commander took the buses from you and would not allow you to go down into the village. What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said actually that all the refugees in Grahovcici were going to the Bila area, controlled by HVO, because they were more safe there, and he told us that they were going to use the buses for this, so they would take the buses and take the refugees from Grahovcici to Bila area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak with the refugees through the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did and they told us that some of them who wanted to go after our first visit, they wanted to go back to the villages, but they were stopped at the checkpoint and forced back by the HVO soldiers up there. The HVO soldiers up there fired warning shots against the Croats who wanted to go back to their houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So against their own people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but only firing in the air; they did not shoot directly on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in the end in this situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the end, we had our buses back and we were able to transport a lot of the refugees back to their own houses. I can remember that 1,400 came back to their own houses, some of them by foot and some of them by the buses. 300 of them decided to stay in Grahovcici and 300 had already been moved or wanted to go to the Bila area, so I think we succeeded in this operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take a seat, please, Major Baggesen. Did you and Henk Morsink reach any conclusions about this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and that conclusion was that people were forced out of the Zenica by HVO spreading those rumours and it was very obvious because we saw, when people wanted to go back, they were forced back by HVO, forced back to that direction where HVO wanted them to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did the HVO want to move them to that area, to the area of Bila?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it was controlled by HVO and it was in the 10th province.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They wanted to increase the population of ethnic Croats in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, because all those villages they came from was in the Bosnian Muslim province number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could just have a moment, Mr. President? (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, continue please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could now again move ahead in time to 27th April, when I think you and Henk Morsink drove to a small Muslim village south of Kiseljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could tender another exhibit, again this is an aerial photograph that has previously been exhibited as exhibit 74. The witness may make some markings of it, so this is a photographic copy. If I could tender that as exhibit 74A and if that could be placed on the easel; thank you. Could you just describe the location of the village of Rotilje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village is situated in this area here and Kiseljak is situated here, and Zenica would be down here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because it is in a northerly direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify a point my colleagues have asked me, who was Henk Morsink?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Henk Morsink was a Dutch monitor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A Dutch army officer serving as a monitor with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You visited the village of Rotilje. Why did you visit the village of Rotilje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we wanted to monitor the situation in the village. There had been an ECMM team in the village before, because there have been some incidents in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What incidents were there in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a Muslim village and there have been some civilians killed in that village by HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to this village, what did you find?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We found that those who were still living in the village were not able to leave the village because the HVO had positions on the slopes of the mountains around the village, so if they tried to go out of the village, there would be some snipers in the area that were firing at them, so they were not able to leave the area; they were not able to get anything in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people in the village soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Women and men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they tell you about events in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing new, nothing we did not know, because we had a team in the area before, but we were told that there had been some killings, very awful things in that village. A young woman was raped and later on slaughtered. It is very difficult to describe how she was slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the court how she was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually what we heard was that after this young woman had been raped an automatic weapon had been put up between her legs and the bullets were fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To which ethnic group did this woman belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom had this action been committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was done by HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told anything else about events in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were told that an elderly couple were burnt alive in the house and two other persons, I think I can remember it was a father and son, they were killed by smashing their head with a skull or an axe or something; it was very awful. We did not see the victims. The former team who visited this area, they saw all the bloodstains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any reason to disbelieve what you had been told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to recall what you have said, the civilians that were left in the village could not leave because snipers were positioned around the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To which force did these snipers belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to now again move forward in time and if I could tender another exhibit, please; this is exhibit 93. This is another ECMM report, I believe written by you. Is that your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this report was created by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, together with the aforementioned Henk Morsink.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that you had actually been told by the ECMM liaison officer which you identified in your testimony yesterday who was stationed at the Kiseljak headquarters of UNPROFOR, of the UN Protection Force, had informed you of certain events in the Kiseljak area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had he told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that something had happened in a small village north of Kiseljak in the Gomionica area. They were able from the UNPROFOR headquarters to see that there were some fires, some houses that were burning up there, and they wanted ECMM to investigate in the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the village of Gomionica on the aerial photograph next to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is this area (indicating) and Kiseljak is up here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could remain standing, Major Baggesen. Mr. President, may I approach the witness? Can you take a pen? Am I correct in saying that you went with an escort from the Canadian battalion of the UN Protection Force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in armoured personnel carriers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is an armoured personnel carrier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an armoured vehicle where normally you are using it to transport people where we need to be protected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It has an armament on it, a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, normally a heavy machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you need to travel in this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we were not safe in our own vehicles because at certain occasions there were shots after us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try and enter the village of Gomionica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We were coming on this direction and we tried the first time to go into Gomionica by using this road, but down here there were a checkpoint manned by a very old man with a very old rifle, but that was not to stop us; we were not allowed to force past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark that checkpoint on the aerial photograph? You have marked it in black marker and you have marked it "HVO CP".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will call it CP1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is fine. So you could not pass by this old man. Who did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was HVO. Therefore we tried another way to the village because we could see another way into the village here. Then we tried to go in here, but we went into another checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was controlling that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark that on the map? For the purposes of the transcript, Major Baggesen is marking another checkpoint and he is marking it "HVO CP2". Could you pass this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not allowed to pass this checkpoint. The soldiers there, they aimed their weapons against us and they aimed their antitank weapons against us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is an antitank weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a weapon you are normally using when you have to kill an armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a shoulder launch weapon, it is a rocket-propelled grenade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these people were serious?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. We were told that the local HVO commander in Kiseljak had ordered them to close all the roads to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he identify who that commander was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but I cannot remember the name. It is in the report, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Baggesen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, he gave us ten seconds to leave that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could pause for a moment, Major Baggesen. (Pause). Am I correct in saying that next you tried to visit the village of Polje Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify that on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was an area over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was another checkpoint and, again, we were stopped at that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark that on the aerial photograph, again with the same marker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot mark the specific position because I cannot remember the specific position, but I can mark the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I would mark the area. If you could mark that "HVO CP3"? For the purposes of the transcript, that is the HVO checkpoint going into the village of Polje Visnjica. Were you able to pass this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not allowed to pass this checkpoint. This time they pulled out mines in front of our armoured vehicles and again they aimed their weapons, including the antitank weapons, against us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they "pulled mines out in front of your vehicle", what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Land mines, so we were not able to pass it with our APC without being killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because the weight of the vehicle would have detonated the mines on the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went back, because we were not able to fulfil our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think now would be actually a good time, if you wish, to finish for this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I agree. We will resume at 2.30 pm. (1.00 pm) (Adjourned until 2.30 pm) 25 (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, for reasons which have been conveyed to me by the Registrar regarding the convenience of the witness, the Chamber will work until 4.30 and after that we will not resume work. So the cross-examination of Mr. Hayman will begin on Monday at 10.00. Mr. Prosecutor, try and finish by 4.30. And anyway that coincides with the time you envisaged for your examination-in-chief, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, your Honours, learned counsel. Two administrative matters arise, Mr. President. First of all, I have received clarification from the Registrar's officer in respect of the diary and the service upon the Defence and I wonder if, Mr. Dubuisson, you could give an account of the movement of that diary in the last year, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Regarding this document, we received a request coming from Mr. Hayman in November. We contacted the translation and it was completed during December. After that, we sent it to Mr. Nobilo in February, together with a number of other documents; that is as far as the first document is concerned, so I recall that what was given yesterday is actually a slightly modified document due to certain translation errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think that clarifies the position, Mr. President, in respect of that document, unless my learned friend has any comments to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I may be permitted to commence my cross-examination on Monday, I do not think there is an issue here to discuss. We are happy to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perfect. The incident is closed. Please continue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The second administrative matter, your Honour, is if I could apply for admission of Prosecutor's exhibits 88, 89A, 89B, 29E, 56A, 50A, 90, 91, 92 and 93 into evidence, please, if there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objections, your Honour, to any of the exhibits marked during this examination. There are some others that counsel mentioned which I cannot call up from memory. We would like to look at those before we waive any objection, just to have in mind what they are. I can list the ones that I think were marked in this examination: 56A, 29E, 50A, 90, 91, 92, 74A, 88 and 89A and 89B, so there is no objection as to those exhibits. The others there may well not be but I would like to make sure I have them all in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which are the others? Excuse me, I did not quite register the exhibits mentioned by Mr. Cayley for which Mr. Hayman is asking for some delay. Maybe I was not paying attention.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, there is first 88 as admitted by Mr. Cayley; it is a map. That is the first map shown this morning. Then we have 89A, which is the English version of the procedural functioning of the ECMM and then the French version of the same, that is B, and that has been mentioned by Mr. Cayley. Then we have the map, 29E, which is actually a copy of map 29 which is to be found on your right, and which was marked by the witness. That is 29E, which was not mentioned by Mr. Cayley. Then exhibit 56A, which is a copy marked by the witness of the map 56. Then the map 50A, again a copy marked by the witness of the map number 50. Then we have exhibit 90, a weekly summary report of Regional Centres; then 91, the mortar photographs; then 92, a two-page document; and 74A, a copy marked by the witness of map 74, that is the last one that is still on the easel, and finally 93, which is a report of the ECMM of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which, Mr. Hayman, are the numbers, following what you have heard from the Registrar, of exhibits you wish to think about? Though I have, each time an exhibit was tendered, asked if there was any objection or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection to those, your Honour. In the order Mr. Cayley read them out, jumping around a little bit, I thought there were some extras in the list. If not, they are all fine with us, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perfect. As everything is fine, Mr. Prosecutor, you can continue with the examination of your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Major Baggesen, we finished your testimony at a point in time where you had tried to visit the village of Polje Visnjica and I think you stated to the court that you were unable to enter that village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I am correct in saying that you then returned to the city of Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to show you another ECMM document. I would like to tender this as Prosecutor's exhibit 94; is that correct? Major Baggesen, do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature at the bottom of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court what the content of this report concerns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually at that day we visited the local Red Cross in Visoko, situated north of Kiseljak and they had a lot of refugees in that area, approximately 20,000 refugees, and 1,038 refugees were coming from the Kiseljak area during the last few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it stated to you where those Bosnian refugees were from, which villages they were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were from Svinjarevo and Jehovac and Gromiljak and Behrici, and from Gomionica and Bilalovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of these villages villages that you had attempted to visit the day before the events that you told us about before lunch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we tried to go into Gomionica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These refugees, were they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that after you had visited these refugees in Visoko, you returned to the Kiseljak area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do when you got to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually we tried to visit the village of Gomionica again and this time, we succeeded to go into the village and a lot of other organisations were waiting to come to the village to see what had happened, so after we came to the village -- no, that was the other day. This day we succeeded to go into the village and when the commander of the two APCs, that was a lieutenant from the Canadian battalion, we dismounted from the APCs, we were fired at from a light machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you made a report, did you not, about these events? I think if I give you that that will assist you in refreshing your memory. If I could tender into evidence Prosecutor's exhibit 94, which is a daily report of 29th April? (Handed). It is 95, my apologies. Do you recognise this report, Major Baggesen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This report concerns your subsequent visit to the Kiseljak area after you had visited the refugees in Visoko. I think you visited a number of villages in the area, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you stand up next to the aerial photograph which I think represents the area, and indicate the location of the village and your findings in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We visited the Gomionica and the Visnjica area. This is the area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are indicating on the area marked Visnjica on that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We visited again this day Gomionica; this was our third attempt to go into the village. The day before, as I mentioned before, we were shot at from some positions in there, but this day there was -- we could go into that area and it was totally -- there were no people in there, no dead bodies, nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the state of the village of Gomionica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lot of burnt houses, but we did not walk because we were afraid that maybe there were some booby-traps, that the area had been mined, so we did not want to go into the buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find in the village of Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Visnjica we found that 40 out of 100 Muslim houses were burnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to it on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not think Doci is marked on that aerial photograph, I do not know if you can remember where it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I cannot remember where it was. In the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is mentioned in your report. The village of Hercezi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is this area here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are pointing to an area of the photograph which is labelled Hercezi. What did you find there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We found that the few Muslim families that returned, they had good relations to the Croat neigbourhoods. There were no burnt houses there, but we were told that there was 14 people killed in the Hercezi area and in the Visnjica area, so in this area between those two we learned that 14 people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you proceed safely through this area on this particular day? Were there any incidences directed against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because there was still the checkpoint and we were stopped in the checkpoint and I can remember that the HVO soldiers there searched our APC and they verbally insulted our Muslim interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which village was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at the checkpoint here marked with "HVO CP3".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other incidences directed against you that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually when we visited Gomionica area, as I was saying before, a lot of other organisations were waiting to come in, and after we came to the area and secured the area with the two Canadian APCs, they had heavy machine-guns and they secured the area because the last time we went there we were shot at, so this time we secured the area. Then we were going in with representatives from UNHCR and from ICRC. During this period, one of the Canadian soldiers observed that some soldiers -- a patrol were in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What soldiers, from the Bosnian army or from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the HVO. This Canadian soldier told us that they were having Droganov, sniper rifle and antitank weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This soldier could observe this HVO patrol with a sniper rifle, I think you said, and an antitank weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: RPG-7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rocket-propelled grenade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything actually happen to you in the village of Gomionica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because after that we went out again because we did not want to get into a conflict with this HVO patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you made a conclusion in your reports, did you not, in respect of all of these villages. Can you read that conclusion to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes: "Our conclusion was it was obvious that ethnic cleansing had taken place in the area."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was obvious that ethnic cleansing had taken place in the area. Do you stand by that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you take a seat, please, Major Baggesen. I would like you to now look at your diary and to refer to the entry on, I think it is Friday 30th April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: To avoid coming back to that, 94, 95, they have already been admitted; there is no objection on the part of the Defence. Very well. Thank you. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This entry I think concerns your visit to the HVO prison in Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court about this incident, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day we went to the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak and we wanted to visit the prison there because there have been a lot of cease-fires down there and there have been a lot of agreements. This time we were going to see if HVO in Kiseljak had fulfilled the latest agreement saying that all prisoners had to be released. In this agreement, it was agreed that all prisoners had to be released at 12.00, and we visited the prison at that time. We were there at 3.00 in the afternoon and we found out that there were still prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now show you the last aerial photograph. The Prosecutor will tender this as exhibit 76A. Again, your Honour, it is a photograph that has already been exhibited and this is a paper copy of the same photograph. Major Baggesen, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a photograph from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you mind if I approached the witness, please? If you could stand up, please, Major Baggesen? If you could wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I apologise. Please continue, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you remember from this photograph where the HVO prison was located in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was located at the Kiseljak barracks, which is situated here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was actually located in the HVO military headquarters in Kiseljak, the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many prisoners were you going there to release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember how many there were, but -- is it mentioned in the diary?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in your diary in fact that there were 48 men held in a 93-metre-squared building. Can you identify in that photograph where those prisoners were held in the Kiseljak area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were some buildings here (indicating), and there were prisoners in that building there and in the building there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With one of these pens, can you ring the building where these prisoners were kept, so you are marking on the photograph in a blue pen the location of the prisoners. Can you write "HVO prison"? Thank you. These prisoners, were they prisoners of war? Were they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember how old they were, but there were old people and young people amongst them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the ages of the young or the elderly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The youngest was a boy of 14 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a boy of 14 years of age in this prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had been told there were some women in there but they had been released earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were they there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was why they were there, because they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Baggesen. Mr. President, I would now like to tender Prosecutor's exhibit 96, which is another ECMM report of 1st May. Mr. President, if there is no objection from my learned friend I would like to move to admit the aerial photograph exhibit 76A into evidence. Major Baggesen, I wonder if you can summarise the contents of this report, again written by you. If I can start you off, I think it concerns a communication, does it not, from the telephone company in Zenica, that the telephone line between Zenica and Sarajevo had been cut and that it had been cut in the Kiseljak area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They wanted you to reconnect the telephone lines so that Zenica could speak with Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started in the morning where we had a meeting at the telephone company's building in Zenica. We had a meeting with the head engineer and he told us that the telephone line was cut in the Kiseljak area and he asked us to do something to get it repaired, because Zenica was not able to make telephone calls to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did he not go and repair the telephone line himself in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the people who were having control over this communication company, PTT, they were Muslims so they were not allowed to go to Kiseljak. They had to pass HVO checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the PTT engineer in Zenica was a Muslim and he could not travel to the PTT offices in Kiseljak because he could not pass through the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose checkpoints were those that he could not pass through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We drove to Kiseljak and we went to the PTT building, the communications building in Kiseljak, to try to investigate in the matter. The building was closed and we were told that the engineer that worked there, he lived in Kresevo and therefore we went to Kresevo to have a meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told in Kiseljak that the telephone engineer who worked there, he lived in Kresevo and that you would need to go there to speak with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did that, and he told us that it was correct that the telephone lines were cut in Kiseljak, and he told us it was due to shelling. There had been some impact, the telephone building had been hit by some grenades, and that is why the PTT line had been broken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The telephone line between Zenica and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he agree to repair the telephone line at Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told us that it would be easy enough to repair the telephone line, it just needed a written order from Colonel Blaskic or a written order from the commander of the HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he would only repair the telephone line in Kiseljak if he received an order from Colonel Blaskic or the head of the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an order from Colonel Blaskic to fix the telephone line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we have not. I can remember we went back to Kiseljak and we went to the Kiseljak barracks and at the HVO headquarters there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO headquarters is the building that you identified on this aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, situated there. We there had a meeting with the head of the PTT in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The head of the telephone company in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was at the headquarters in Kiseljak. He told us the same, that the telephone line was cut due to the shelling at the building. He furthermore told us that he could not see any reason to repair it because it was not necessary for Zenica to have any contact with Sarajevo. He did not want to repair that before after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He said that he saw no need for Zenica to be able to communicate with Sarajevo and that in any event he would not see it should be repaired until after the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was his own personal opinion but I think if we had the written order from Colonel Blaskic or from the commander of the military police, he had to repair it. When we saw this PTT building in Kiseljak, we only saw a small impact, a small damage at the building, and I do not think that was enough to damage all the technics in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were suspicious about whether or not it had been damaged by shellfire or whether or not it had been deliberately cut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That it had been cut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Deliberately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could turn to your diary entry of 7th May, which concerns the establishment of a joint headquarters in the Kiseljak area, a joint headquarters of the HVO and the BiH. What do you recall about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can recall at this time yesterday I was speaking about the Busovaca Joint Commission and at this time, this was replaced by a joint headquarters in the Travnik area and now we want to make a similar joint headquarters in the Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the Busovaca Joint Commission which was a sort of commission where the two parties talked to each other was replaced in the Vitez and Travnik area by a joint military headquarters, by a military headquarters between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was organised by negotiation through your body, the ECMM, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wanted to do the same thing in Kiseljak; is that correct? You wanted to set up a joint military headquarters between the Bosnian army and the HVO in Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court about the meeting concerning that joint headquarters, and whether or not it was ever set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had the meeting at UNPROFOR headquarters in Kiseljak with participations from HVO and BiH, and from UNPROFOR, and we were trying to establish this joint headquarters. It was a long meeting and I mentioned in my diary that it lasted six hours, and we were not able to go anywhere during this meeting. The BiH, they wanted to co-operate and they wanted that we should make this mixed headquarters, but the HVO did not want to make this joint headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, why did the HVO not want a joint headquarters in the Kiseljak area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because at that time HVO were controlling that area. They do not want to share this command with BiH. I think the reason for BiH at that time wanted to co-operate was because they were the weak part and they actually were fighting with their back against the wall, so this was their only way to survive in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could look at your diary entry for 8th May you visited an area I think called Fojnica. Where is Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We do not have a map of it, but just describe to the court in relation to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is close to Kiseljak, South West of Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Fojnica, what did you discover there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything was quiet, people were living together, Croats and Muslims working together without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the Prosecutor could tender exhibit 97 to the witness. Do you recognise this report, Major Baggesen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I direct you to 3D on that report. This was an incident which I think happened on 11th May, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain this incident to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I will start a little earlier, because at this time, as I mentioned before, this joint headquarters was established in the Travnik area, and that morning, I went to visit this joint headquarters together with a Greek monitor, Stavros Kinigopoulos, and we went to the joint headquarters and at the headquarters we were told about some incidents, and one of the incidents they told us about was an HVO soldier had been killed by a sniper, and old Croat civilian men had been killed and there have been fightings between two units of BiH and HVO. While we were there we were told that some Muslim families were forced out of their houses in the Novoj Biloj area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is close to Vitez. We went to that area and we witnessed that two Muslim families were forced out of their houses and their houses were given over to Croat families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who forced them out of their houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an HVO unit, we were able to see that, and we were told the commander of this HVO unit had the nickname Zuti. We heard this name in other occasions as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you witness this event actually happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you not try to stop the eviction of this people from their house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very difficult for us to stop things happening down there because we were unarmed, we could only do it verbally. It is very difficult to negotiate with a man carrying a rifle, so we complained about this and this was everything we were able to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you complain to about this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On our way back we passed Colonel Blaskic and we complained about this to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you passed Colonel Blaskic. You passed the hotel Vitez in Vitez and you went into his headquarters and you told him about this incident. What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said he was sorry and he would try to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think because at this time it only seems as a minor problem that two families were forced out. I am sorry to say, but that was the reality down there. It was not the last time we saw people forced out of their own houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think if we move forward again in time to 14th May, you had a meeting again at this new joint headquarters between the Bosnian army and the HVO in Travnik, and I think at that time you asked representatives of the Bosnian army and representatives of the HVO for a list of all of the units in their area and the person under whose command those units fell. Did you ever receive that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received a list from HVO that was handed over to me at the spot and later translated by my interpreter to an English list. I did not receive a list from BiH at the spot, so I have not seen the list from BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could tender Prosecutor's exhibit 98. (Handed). Do you recognise this list, Major Baggesen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This list shows the name of the commanders for the units that were under Colonel Blaskic's command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was provided to you by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a translation my interpreter did at the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the original document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this lists all the brigades under his command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is telling the name of the brigade, the commander's name actually, their telephone numbers for the headquarters and where they were located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any particular comments to make about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it shows that as I told you earlier these units Colonel Blaskic was commanding were organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could take you forward to 10th June and the entry in your diary for that day, I think at this time there had been a major cease-fire agreement in Bosnia; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It had been signed by the UNPROFOR commander on the ground and also by Brigadier General Petkovic, the Chief of Staff of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that part of that agreement was an agreement by both sides for the release of prisoners of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you were appointed as the chairman of the commission that would oversee the release of those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to add that this agreement was signed by BiH as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who signed it on behalf of the Bosnian army, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but it was not Hadzihasanovic but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His superior, so the Commander in Chief of the Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that on 15th June, you had the opportunity to visit the HVO police chief in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was his headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the old cinema Vitez, very close to the HVO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was the cinema from the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you go to visit the Vitez cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because this joint humanitarian commission which I was the chairman for, we were going to visit all places where we had heard rumours that there should be some detained persons or where there should be prisoners, so therefore we started off to visit all those places, and there were some rumours that there were some prisoners at the police station, therefore we went to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to the HVO personnel about these rumours in the police station in the Vitez cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had a meeting with the commander there for the police, and he told us that there were no prisoners in the police station. Then I told him that this joint humanitarian commission was allowed to seek all areas. As far as I can remember, we even had a piece of paper that we showed him, then we were allowed to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the piece of paper signed by; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was signed by the before-mentioned Generals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the original cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After the police commander had seen this paper and before we even had to search the area he told us, okay, he had five persons in the basement, down in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go down to the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We found that there were five Muslims sitting down there in a small room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Poor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they prisoners of war, soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Males, females?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Males. They told us they came from Banja Luka; they were on their way to Zenica but they were taken into custody at an HVO checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were refugees from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked the HVO representative in the commission to release them at the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: A bit more slowly please, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I am watching the clock. I will slow down. You say you released them on the spot. Where did you take them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, we took them back to Zenica and we gave them to the International Red Cross who had headquarters in Zenica and they have a desk where refugees could sign in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are quite sure that these people were civilians that were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, no doubt. I think one of them was too young to be a soldier and the rest of them were too old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now take you to your diary entry of 21st June, I think at this time you returned to Kiseljak again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was in respect of your duties as the chairman of this prisoner release, this humanitarian commission to release prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to the prison in Kiseljak at the HVO barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point to that on the photograph that is up there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To this area, where we have been before (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a military headquarters as well as a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under whose command did this fall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the prison, were you expecting to receive some Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had been very difficult to work in that area because we had tried several days to come into Kiseljak prison to release those prisoners. In the beginning, we were allowed to go in there from the commission, but before we were able to release the prisoners, the International Red Cross had to interview all prisoners before we were able to release them, but the International Red Cross were not allowed to come into the prison, so therefore -- we could not release them before the ICRC, International Red Cross, had interviewed the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this occasion, you were able to release the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you able to do it on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this occasion, because of all the problems we had down there, we were always -- because at this time, there have been some conflict between Muslims and Croats and there have been some fightings in the Kresevo area, and therefore, we were told that the local commander down there, he was at the front in Kresevo and therefore there were no men down there who were able to authorise the release, but one of the days the HVO member of the commission went to Colonel Blaskic and had a written order from Colonel Blaskic that ICRC should be allowed to visit the prison, so after some bureaucracy, we were able to go in there and we were able to release the 66 prisoners on this Monday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived, what did the HVO commander at the Kiseljak barracks say to you about the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived that morning, actually he told us that the prisoners had already been released. Then I asked him for a piece of paper that could certify that they have been released, and then he said, "Okay, they are not released; they are working in the field."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
