utterances.text: I was not able to see any fields in the area and there was no -- I could not see any farms. Then he told me that they were -- he only used the word "fieldworking" because they were out digging trenches and clearing minefields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these prisoners were out digging trenches and clearing minefields; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO commander at Kiseljak informed you of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say to him when he told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tried to give him a lecture on the Geneva Convention, but he told me that you cannot use it down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He told you that the Geneva Conventions did not apply to the Kiseljak area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these prisoners ever arrive in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we had to wait for ten hours and then they came back and in the beginning there were only 65 and then we ask for the last one and again we were told that he was released this morning, but when we asked for a piece of paper that could clarify this, he said, "Okay, he is working in the field too", but he was in another place. After a while, we received the last man and we were able to go back with all 66 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these individuals prisoners of war, combatants, or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were all civilians these people that were released to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take you to your diary entry of 23rd June? If you could explain your entry concerning the village of Skradno where you state in your diary the HVO held 88 Muslims, where is the village of Skradno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Skradno is situated east of Vitez, in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You visited it on 23rd June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did and we have heard that there was some Muslims living in that area, but all those Muslims in that area came from another area, and I think it was named not Busovaca but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bukovici. So all the Muslims in Skradno were from a village called Bukovici. Why were they being held in Skradno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I do not know, but the HVO had moved them to Skradno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they concerned, these Muslims, in the village of Skradno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because you are not able to leave Skradno because there were some HVO guards in the area, not in Skradno but in the surrounding area, so you are not able to leave the area, and they were afraid and there were those rumours that Skradno would be a new Ahmici if BiH attacked Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If there are no objections from my learned friend, I would like to admit exhibits 96, 97 and 98 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Registrar, they have been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, what date did you leave Bosnia; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left Zenica at 28th June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some concluding remarks, based on your experiences in Bosnia and your expertise as a career army officer in the Danish Army. Of the two sides, the HVO and the BiH, who was better armed, in your opinion, from what you saw on the ground during your time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very obvious that HVO were better equipped and they have more weapons than their counterparts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is from your observations on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which of the two armies resembled more of a standard military unit? In that sense, I mean an organised military unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no doubt that HVO were a well organised unit, so I think that Colonel Blaskic had a well organised unit, and we could see that when we saw the list with all the brigades and all the commanders, that this was a well organised unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your impression over those months, you felt that the HVO was a well organised army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area where I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Discipline. Which of the two armies, the Bosnian army or the HVO were a better disciplined unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer on this one, but actually I think BiH were the best disciplined army of those two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I think the soldiers were more -- I cannot use the word "polite", but they were more like soldiers, they were acting more like soldiers, they have -- I think their morale was a little better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was their morale better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I think that the officers in the BiH, they were able to encourage their soldiers. They had to, because at that time, BiH, they were a beaten army, and the only way a beaten army can survive is by their officers to encourage the soldiers trying to ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to encourage your soldiers in what is a fairly desperate situation; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of training, did you see any training of HVO soldiers going on whilst you were down in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I do not know, because normally you had to train your soldiers, even if there is a war going on, but any time when we visited some of the headquarters at the barracks, we did not see any training or anything similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to recap, to go back: the attacks which you witnessed, the attack of which you witnessed the aftermath in Ahmici and the attack which you witnessed ongoing in Vitez, and in fact you also witnessed the aftermath of attacks in the Kiseljak area -- what type of organisation do you need to mount military operations of that size and that scale over that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the attack against Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that attack, as I said earlier, I think 500 to 600 men; that is a battalion, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does an attack like that involve planning from a high level within a military unit, normally speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because every military operation had to be planned if you want a result, and a good result where you have to take care of -- you have to take care of all the things. You have to bring in ammunition, you have to bring in the soldiers and you have to plan for all those things, planning for the communications and different things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that in most armed forces, there are agreed orders, whether they be oral or written, which actually cover every aspect that is necessary for a military operation to reduce casualties, to bring in ammunition, to bring in fuel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is normal for an army unit to have that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think that the attacks that you saw would have had to have been organised and well organised at a high level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the three months that you were in Central Bosnia and in the Vitez area, Vitez and Kiseljak, can you recall, and only if you recall, whether you saw in those areas during those three months generally more HVO soldiers, generally more Bosnian army soldiers or about the same number of both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those mentioned areas, there were generally more HVO soldiers than BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the Zenica municipality or the city of Zenica, were there more HVO or more Bosnian army or about the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, there were only BiH soldiers in Zenica. In the beginning, there were two HVO brigades in the Zenica area, but they lay down their weapons, so there were only BiH soldiers in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just on your own personal expertise, I think you have a number of badges on your right chest which indicate that you are a specialist in certain fields in the army. I wonder if you could just, concentrating on those concerning weapons and communications, if you could indicate by pointing to your chest what those badges mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The different ones here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specialist badges on different kinds of weapons, small arms, and specialist badge in communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are a recognised expert to a degree in the Danish Army in those particular areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have a number of decorations for distinguished service in the Danish Army, do you not, on your right chest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually it is only one of them from Denmark; the rest of them are --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For UN service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Baggesen. Mr. President, I do not have any further questions of the witness, so I offer him to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, though we said that the cross-examination would begin Monday, if you are ready, the Trial Chamber would be grateful to you if you could help us to make some progress and work until 4.30. Of course, that would be convenient for the witness who would be able to go home after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I leave it to the court, your Honour. I can start but what I would have to warn the court is that I have not yet had an opportunity to compare the 33-page diary with this witness's other statements, so, if I start today, then Monday when I have compared them I may have to go back and ask the witness about the same events, having had a chance to review this diary and compare it to the other statements, but I can begin. I am happy to, but I, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am going to consult my colleagues. (Pause). The Trial Chamber has decided to continue, so it is your turn, Mr. Hayman. Of course, it is understood that if it is necessary for some further clarifications after having studied the documents, you will be able to do so. Therefore please begin, Mr. Hayman. Cross-examined by MR. HAYMAN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good afternoon, major. Do you recall receiving a letter from me some months ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not have it in front of me, so bear with me. In that letter, did I request the opportunity to meet with you and interview you before the trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of receiving that letter, did you consult with authorities in your government concerning that possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the government, because I have not received anything from my government about your letter, but I was discussing it with the Danish military advocate judge, and we were told -- I can tell you why; in Denmark we have other rules than here. In Denmark, it is the police who are the prosecutors, and they are -- if I were and I was told I have to be the Prosecutor's witness, then the defence were not allowed to speak with me, and that is why we did not have the opportunity to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were told by the judge advocate or the judge within the military court or law department that you conferred with that under Danish national law or the law of the Danish military, you were forbidden from talking to the Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not forbidden, but it was advised by him that this was the Danish rules and we did not know the rules of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you knew that someone else was going to respond to me and tell me that in essence it was forbidden for you to speak with me under the Danish rules or the Danish practice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you, I do not know. I was called several times from your office in Los Angeles and I told this to this lady who called me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You relayed this to Miss van Essen yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that was her name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that this same policy has been applied to other former ECMM monitors from Denmark, that they are not allowed to speak with the Defence; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that you already had our statements so you had the information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of them, yes. Tell me, the Home Guard in Denmark: how frequently do the Home Guard soldiers train?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It all depends on what kind of unit. Normally, they have exercises once a month for a weekend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similar to what we would call the Army Reserve in the United States?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe similar to your National Guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. These soldiers in the Home Guard, they are not full-time professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they are not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it particularly important where soldiers do not have professional training, that is they have not served on a full-time basis in the military, that they have regular training opportunities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you do not have that, you do not really have soldiers, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Danish Home Guard, we have a lot of tasks -- we do not only use the soldiers for fighting, we have Home Guard soldiers who are doing other things like that, who are specialists in sitting in an office and doing all those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about fighting now. If you take a civilian and call him a soldier and do not give him any training and no regular training opportunities, you do not really have a soldier, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Normally, when we are going to have the new Home Guard soldiers, a lot of them have been soldiers -- we have national service in Denmark and a lot of the Home Guard soldiers have already been given that military training in the army. After that, a lot of them volunteer to the Home Guard. Those who have not been in the army, we normally -- we always give them a basic training in the beginning just after they have signed their contract with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long does that basic training last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We gave them one week in use of weaponry. This first week includes classes in the law, fighting in -- I cannot remember the name now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fighting in built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not built-up areas. When you have in a conflict -- the rules --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, is that very important for the Defence of General Blaskic, to know the system of military training in Denmark? If it is important, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will move as rapidly as I can, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To have an effective military, you need absolute adherence to the chain of command, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because if you do not have that, you have people doing what they want to do, not what they have been ordered to do; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it all depends on your military commanders. If you had a good military commander, you will have good superior -- you have some good officers and you will have some good soldiers, if you have a good commander, because the commander, his responsibility to his commander is the discipline and the morale, if these two is perfect. His battalion or brigade commanders are responsible to him for the training and all that, so every commander on the different levels are responsible for the training and the morale, the discipline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the soldiers in the field, they are responsible to their first or immediate commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then that commander is in turn responsible to superior commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for a person in the position of then Colonel Blaskic, the individuals that he was directly responsible for directing their behaviour were his brigade commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were responsible to Colonel Blaskic that his men behave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was responsible for telling them what he expected of them and how he expected their men to behave and conduct themselves; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does a soldier acquire this ethos, if you will, of adherence to the chain of command? How do you instil that in a new soldier or recruit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is normally not a problem, because when you teach soldiers then you -- it is very easy to teach them on the chain of command. They know that they have to do what they are told to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is when you are bringing soldiers into an existing army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They can see how other soldiers behave. Imagine a situation, if you would, where there is no existing army but a large group of people are gathered together and said, "We are under attack; you have to become an army", but there are no or few role models in terms of adhering to this chain of command. Can you imagine in that situation it might be more difficult instilling in these soldiers an ethos in which they are committed to adhering to a chain of command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It all depends on the people's discipline and their morale. It is no excuse. If you are going to have an armed force and it is only people who have never been given a weapon before, you are still responsible for giving that training. The commander is always the man who is responsible for what his men are doing. So it is not an excuse if you go to war with a lot of people who are not having their basic training, because those soldiers who you are giving those weapons to can do a lot of awful things with those weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are using the term "not an excuse". Not an excuse in terms of what normative or legal structure?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I object, your Honour? Counsel is now talking about "normative" and "legal" structures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not hear that. My microphone was not switched on properly. Could you please repeat your objection, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have two points to make. The first point is counsel is using the words "within what normative or legal structure". First of all, this witness is a military man; he is giving his opinion on the organisation of armies, and, secondly, Defence counsel is well aware that English is not this witness's first language. He does speak like many Scandinavians good English, but using phrases like that is going to confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I do not really understand very well your second remark which I do not think is quite permanent. As for the first, my impression was that the witness has already answered that question, so perhaps we can hurry it on a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think so, your Honour. Can I say, major, if at any time I use expressions or words that are unclear to you please stop me, because the last thing I want to do is elicit any information from you that is not totally accurate and does not completely represent your testimony before this Tribunal. Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the concept of fighting in built-up areas. Is fighting in built-up areas sometimes necessary, for example if the military objective of the operation is to gain control of a town with a high density or a high number of buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes, it can be necessary to fight in built-up areas, but normally all units are doing their best to avoid this, because when you have to fight in built-up areas, it is a big risk because there is a lot of civilians in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is one option where fighting in built-up areas is necessary to try and remove the civilian population, either by invitation or by force so that they are removed from the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a way you can do it, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that does not occur and yet the fighting occurs, is it inevitable, however tragic, that there will be civilian casualties in the course of that fighting in built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I think you are going to have a very very, very good excuse to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It has to be absolutely necessary in the sense of military necessity; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot imagine what the reasons would be that are good enough to kill civilian people, just to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it were necessary -- and if you are not comfortable answering the question, that is fine, you can say so -- if it were necessary and fighting in built-up areas occurs, would you agree that civilian casualties, however tragic, are inevitable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact it is likely that more civilians than soldiers will be killed as a result of such fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That could be the result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days were you on the ground in Bosnia in the course of your service as an EC monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How many days?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long? What exactly was the time-period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you can see in the diary, I arrived in the Zenica area on 2nd April, and we went home early morning on Monday, 28th June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any leave or recreation period while you were in country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went home for a week to Denmark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So altogether that means you spent about ten weeks in country on duty as an EC monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you normally reside in Zenica during your period of service? Is that where you were bunked or quartered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many nights during your ten weeks in Bosnia-Herzegovina did you spend in Vitez; that is, how many times did you overnight in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall, because normally at our house in Vitez, during the night there were one monitor and one interpreter, but I cannot recall how many nights I spent in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate: was it a few days, or a week or two, or half of your time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe five or six nights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have office duty on any days as, say, the operations manager or operations officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a regular rotation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not because normally I was in the field as a team leader. A few days we were sitting at the headquarters in Zenica making reports. Sometimes we were sitting in the house in Vitez and made those reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of your briefing on arrival first in Zagreb and then in Zenica. When you arrived and you received this briefing, were you briefed on the threat that the Serbs were posing to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told about that conflict as well. Actually, we were told that close to a front against the Bosnian Serb Army, normally BiH and HVO were working together in those areas without problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that the HVO and the BiH together were virtually encircled by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not totally, because HVO had borders to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They could take the road down through Gornji Vakuf and out to Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But other than that roadway, were the Croats and Muslims, if you will, in Central Bosnia encircled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you briefed or did you learn in the course of your service what the rough population mix in this pocket, if you will, in Central Bosnia was; was it 5:1 Muslims to Serbs, 10:1, 2:1, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can remember that we saw something on that, and somewhere, and I still have that, I have a piece of paper telling how the ethnic groups -- how many there were in the different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have no recollection of an aggregate number on that score?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At your briefing in Zenica, you said you were told who the military commanders were of the army and the HVO. What were you told in that briefing about Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that he was Vice-President of Herceg-Bosna, and he was the local political leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That he liked to dress in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you told, if anything, in that briefing concerning HOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told about HOS that it was a military unit with connection to the Croatian army. We were told that they were better trained and they were better equipped, i.e. they had better and more modern weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it explained to you that they were separate from the HVO when you arrived and got this briefing; that they were a separate entity from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn after arriving in Zenica that there was an HOS unit in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember where we saw those HOS units, but we saw them different places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a HOS unit in Zenica that was part of the army of BiH when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that, that there had been such a unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of -- and I am jumping ahead a little bit in your testimony; let me warn you of that -- that on one occasion at a checkpoint you saw the HOS flag and it was a black skull and crossbones flag; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that HOS were known to commit certain types of acts. Can you tell us more about that? What kinds of acts were you either told or did you come to know HOS members were prone to or likely to commit, if I am stating it accurately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that the HOS units normally were those units that were used when you have to -- when HVO were going to do some of the dirty work. By that, I mean when they are going to burn houses and kill civilians and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that they were prone to commit criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you use another word for that, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will; thank you for asking. Were you told that they were likely to commit criminal acts because of the characteristics or the traits that they held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told anything in your briefings or did you learn anything during your service about an individual named Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told anything in your briefings or did you learn anything during your service in the country concerning a unit named Vitezovi, or the Vitez Knights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you the same question concerning a unit known as the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard about that unit, but I was not able to recognise them. I know they have a special badge, but I have not seen people wearing this badge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn anything else about them during your service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not during my service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your service concluded, did you learn anything about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That it was a special unit, that they had contact to the HVO military police, and that they were doing crimes against human rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you met with then Colonel Blaskic ten or fifteen times during your tour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On one occasion you said you met him at the Easter celebration in Vitez on April 12th 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On another occasion you said you met him and you obtained an order from him for the release of a certain number of prisoners in Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have the meeting concerning that. The HVO representative in the Joint Humanitarian Commission went to Colonel Blaskic to get this permission, or one of the HVO members of the commission had this written order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which member was that that went and got that order from Colonel Blaskic, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Concerning the release --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The release of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which of the releases?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one concerning the prisoners in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The big release.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The big release at the end when you finally got the prisoners out of prison utilising an order you got from Colonel Blaskic, you finally got an order to get them out. Do you remember which representative got that order for the joint commission. Was it Zoran Mr.avak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, or Pero Skopljak because the other two persons in the humanitarian commission went into an ambush on their way to Vitez to get a written order. I cannot remember if it was those two who were going to have this written order, but we had the written order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two other members of the HVO joint commission were ambushed on the way to Vitez that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on that day, but I have mentioned that in the diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the way to Skradno? Are you thinking of June 23rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that day we had a meeting in Busovaca first, and then we were going to have some papers, so this was -- I do not think this was that they were going to -- they were not going for the Kiseljak papers. I think they were going to get another piece of paper, but they went into an ambush.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are recalling, I take it, that on 23rd June 1993, two HVO members of this joint commission -- and by the way, had these two been working with you for some time to try and resolve problems and reduce tensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have met them before because there have been members in the Busovaca Joint Commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were not full-time members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them, I cannot recall his name, I cannot remember if it was Zoran Mr.avak or it was Zarko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You left them in Busovaca; you stayed to do something and they went ahead to Vitez, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Normally, at that time, we were provided with an armed escort from the British battalion. When we were driving in a Croat-occupied area, the two Muslim or three Muslim representatives in the Commission was sitting inside this APC, so they were secure and when we were travelling to a Muslim-controlled area, the HVO members were sitting in the APC. That is why the two HVO members were driving in their own vehicle because they were driving in an HVO-controlled area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even though they were in HVO-controlled territory on 23rd June 1993, nonetheless, they were ambushed by Mujahedin fighters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of them was killed on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other was seriously injured in his legs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was in fact very dangerous in the area you were moving around in during May and June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Extremely dangerous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you moved only in an armoured vehicle of some sort during that period of time, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have armoured vehicles, sometimes we had to do it in a soft skin vehicle. We preferred to have an armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the occasion, coming back to this order for the release of the prisoners in Kiseljak, you did not actually have a meeting with Colonel Blaskic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you met with him ten or fifteen times. Can you identify the first time you met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the first time. I think I met Colonel Blaskic before the Easter celebration, but I cannot remember the exact time, because when I say I met Colonel Blaskic ten or fifteen times, I did not speak to him all those times. Maybe we were together in another team, i.e. the Busovaca Joint Commission and other monitors from the Busovaca Joint Commission was speaking to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he attend any meetings of the Busovaca Joint Commission at which you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can remember actually him attending some of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say you can or you cannot remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, was that one or more than one meeting that he attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall but at that stage one or two meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember anything discussed, what the subject matter of that meeting or two meetings was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot, but normally if Colonel Blaskic were at our meetings, normally Hadzihasanovic would be at the same meeting and we were normally at this level discussing a local cease-fire agreement, and, as I told you before, or I told the Prosecutor, there was made a lot of agreements and cease-fires down there so I cannot recall them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other substantive meetings with Colonel Blaskic; that is not meetings where perhaps a cup of coffee was had and pleasantries exchanged but any actual discussions, either that you participated in or that you were present, when other people had substantive discussions with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall them all. I can recall having met Colonel Blaskic ten or fifteen times. That is as I told you -- it is not necessarily that I had a meeting, but I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I read your diary, I could perhaps direct you to anything that may be in here; I will read it before we continue on Monday, and I will end this area soon, but do you remember any substantive meetings or substantive discussions that you attended or participated in with then Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, normally if we had something where we want to speak, we have to make a complaint, a big complaint to Colonel Blaskic or to the Commander of the 3rd Muslim Corps, Hadzihasanovic, normally it was not done by a monitor but by an ambassador.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thebault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Thebault have free and complete access to make complaints or register information with then Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I do not think that it was easier for the ambassador that it was for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of access did you or your colleagues on the monitoring mission have then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally if we were going to have a meeting with Colonel Blaskic -- actually we were not able to call him from Zenica, so we had to go to his headquarters and he was not always in, so therefore ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When there was something that needed to be brought to his attention, was ECMM able to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, normally when we were sitting in the Busovaca Joint Commission there was a lot of complaints and normally they were giving to Franjo Nakic, who was Colonel Blaskic's deputy; then Mr. Nakic was supposed to give them to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get to know Franjo Nakic well in the course of working with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not be able to know a man well during this short period, but I think that Mr. Nakic was a man who we could trust.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you feel that he was doing his best to try and make the Joint Commission work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware he was hand-picked for the job by Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware that he was Colonel Blaskic's deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I suppose that is the reason for him sitting in the Busovaca Joint Commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was misconduct by drunken soldiers a continuing problem during your tour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a problem to me; it was a problem to the people down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a problem to all the residents of the area, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not every day, especially in the beginning, in the Easter, the soldiers on both sides actually had something to drink and then they fight with weapons normally in the air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not always?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke to us concerning the Vance-Owen Plan, and you told us that you personally were afraid of what fruit the Vance-Owen Plan might produce. Do you believe that the Vance-Owen Plan caused the civil authorities in Central Bosnia to have less incentive to try and work together and form a joint authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Vance-Owen Plan have an effect on the Croat citizenry of Central Bosnia, if you know? I am talking of the average man.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I think that all the people down there were -- they heard a lot of new agreements and a new cease-fire and all that. Honestly I think that the Vance-Owen Plan for the people down there was just another plan that would be replaced by another plan that would be replaced by another plan, so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not think that there was an understanding among many citizens that the international community had given Croats in the 10th province the right to govern that province?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe for the Croats in that area, if they came from that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it definitely increase tensions between Croats and Muslims in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke to us of a flag-raising incident on or about April 12th. Do you know any more about what actually happened in Travnik, I believe it was, in connection with that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can remember that there was a lot of tension in that area, but it was not my area of responsibility. I can remember that there were a lot of problems in the Travnik area because of the flag-raising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you if any of this stimulates your memory. Were one or more Croatian flags raised as part of an Easter celebration? Does that refresh any recollection in your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were told, it was not raised only because of the Easter celebration, it was raised because the Croat inhabitants wanted to use the Croat flag when they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told it by the Croats in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croats in Travnik told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you what happened to the flags that were raised? Were they taken down and burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should not be surprised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then there was some shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that does not stimulate your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because it was not my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You told us of the kidnapping of four HVO officers that you learned of on April 14th 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that they were kidnapped near the front, close to Travnik. That front was a front with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I cannot remember the exact place where they were kidnapped, I can just remember it was in the Travnik area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already said that the situation was extremely tense in Travnik. Did the kidnapping of these four officers worsen those tensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went, together with Nakic and Merdan and others to visit the 7th Muslim Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that brigade? Were there any special characteristics of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say. The 7th Muslim Brigade was a brigade -- one of the brigades under Hadzihasanovic's command. It was different to the others because this brigade were manned by Muslims who were more Islamic than the rest of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was religious fervour a common bond among the men in that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and they were all looking very Islamic, they were all having a beard and normally they were using great banners with Islamic words on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Arabic words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were soldiers from Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you and the other members of the investigative team went to the 7th Muslim Brigade. Did Merdan, General Merdan or whatever his proper title was at the time, concur that the 7th Muslim Brigade should be visited to enquire about the kidnapping of these four officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was the one that suggested that you have to go there, so we went there, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that after they denied any knowledge or involvement in the kidnappings, you left, but the phrase you used was, "We did not trust them 100 per cent." Can you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I said: we did not trust them 100 per cent. By that, I meant we maybe believed them 99 per cent. We were a little -- because they were very different to all the other kinds of units we had meetings with and they acted in another way, so we were -- we did not know where we had them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to Bosnian Croats in Central Bosnia and determine whether the 7th Muslim Brigade inspired great fear among the Croats in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did, because there was a lot of rumours, especially spread by HVO, that the 7th Muslim Brigade were doing a lot of naughty things down there. So again we saw HVO and were telling lots of stories about what the 7th Muslim Brigade did, so it is natural people were scared of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And people were scared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People were scared. Everyone was scared down there, even me sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us after your visit to the 7th Muslim Brigade you went back to the HVO brigade command in Novi Travnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There a military policeman took certain acts. Was that the local military commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember if he was the local military police commander or he was -- at which level he was a commander, but he was a high rank officer, I think. I was surprised that Nakic -- either Nakic or Mr. Sabljic, the local brigade commander, were able to order him to release us again. Therefore we concluded that he was a high rank officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with that incident, did the HVO military police officer -- did he also place Nakic under arrest, Franjo Nakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Nakic free to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because he was together with us in our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You all stayed in the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at Mr. Sabljic's office; we were sitting all in his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there another HVO representative or was Nakic the only one with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nakic was the only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He stayed with you and Merdan while the situation got worked out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And Mr. Sabljic, the HVO brigade commander, was there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic and Mr. Sabljic, were they very unhappy with the actions of this military policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. As I said before, they told us they were unable to do anything because the military police were not under their command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they said that, "not under their command", you knew Nakic was the deputy for the Operative Zone Central Bosnia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the military police did not report to the Operative Zone Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because we were told by Nakic -- I cannot remember if it was Nakic or Sabljic -- that the only one who was able to command the military police was Colonel Blaskic. That was the reason for us to call Colonel Blaskic. If we knew that this unit was not under his command, we would have tried to call another one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say that Colonel Blaskic was the only one who might be able to get Merdan out in substance; is that what they said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said that Colonel Blaskic commanded the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were speaking through an interpreter, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Nakic and Sabljic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had an interpreter with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day we have our senior interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was the phone conversation or conversations between then Colonel Blaskic and this military policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the Commander's Office, I think a few minutes, then he went to another office to continue the conversation in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was he absent in this other office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember, five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, all told, it was somewhere in excess of ten minutes on the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before he came back and the release was effected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps we should adjourn now, because I think the witness has some personal business, and we will meet again on Monday at 10.00. Thank you. (4.35 pm) (Court adjourned until 10.00 am on Monday, 25th August 1997) 22 23 24 25
